name: Causality (as theoretical framework)
description: The theoretical framework and principles that define cause-and-effect relationships, often formalized through models. Provides abstract conceptual system for reasoning about influence, intervention, and explanation.

chronology.summary: Causality as a philosophical concept dates back to Plato and Aristotle. Modern causal frameworks emerged from Hume's regularity theory, later extended by counterfactual, probabilistic, and interventionist approaches. Since the 1990s, formal graphical and structural models (Pearl, Rubin) have dominated.

events.event: Aristotle formulates the Four Causes
Hume publishes 'A Treatise of Human Nature', regularity theory of causation
Lewis publishes 'Causation', counterfactual theory
Pearl introduces causal diagrams and do-calculus

relationships.description: This framework is a subtype of the abstract category Epistemic Framework.
This framework formalizes the causal model blueprint.

specific.coreAssumptions: Causality involves counterfactual dependence, intervention, and graphical structure
specific.integrationScope: Allows reasoning about cause-effect in science

name: Causal Model (generic representation scheme)
description: A representation of the relationships between variables in a system, aiming to understand how changes in one variable can influence or cause changes in other variables.

chronology.summary: Generic causal models have been used in science since at least the 20th century, with path analysis (Wright) as an early precursor. The modern notion of a formal causal model crystallized with structural equation modeling and graphical approaches.

events.event: Wright introduces path analysis
Structural equation models become widespread in social sciences
Pearl's 'Causality' book formalizes causal models as DAGs + structural equations

relationships.description: This blueprint is a subtype of the abstract category Epistemic Blueprint.

expressiveLimits: acyclic
no latent feedback

name: Structural Causal Model (SCM)
description: Uses directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and structural equations to represent and compute counterfactuals. A specific formalism within causal modeling.

chronology.summary: SCM was formalized by Judea Pearl in the 1990s, building on earlier work on graphical models, structural equations, and causal Bayesian networks. It became the dominant framework for counterfactual and interventionist reasoning.

events.event: Pearl introduces SCM in 'Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research'
Publication of 'Causality: Models, Reasoning, and Inference'
Second edition of 'Causality' includes extensive SCM developments

relationships.description: This blueprint is a subtype of the generic causal model blueprint.

expressiveLimits: acyclic
deterministic functions

name: Do-calculus
description: Algebraic rules for reasoning about interventions and identifying causal effects from observational data.

chronology.summary: Do-calculus was developed by Judea Pearl in the mid‑1990s as a set of three rules to derive causal effects from graphical models. It provides the mathematical foundation for identifying interventions without running experiments.

events.event: Pearl introduces do-calculus in 'Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research'
Do-calculus presented systematically in 'Causality'
Shpitser and Pearl prove completeness of do-calculus

relationships.description: This operator is a subtype of the abstract category Epistemic Operator.
Do-calculus acts on causal models to identify interventions.

specific.transformationRule: three rules for manipulating conditional probabilities under interventions

name: Counterfactual Reasoning
description: Reasoning about hypothetical outcomes under alternative scenarios; defining causation in terms of difference-making.

chronology.summary: Counterfactual reasoning has roots in Hume and was formalized by Lewis (1973). Pearl integrated it with SCM, operationalizing counterfactuals through structural equations. It is now central to causal inference and AI explainability.

events.event: Hume discusses counterfactuals in 'An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding'
Lewis publishes 'Causation' using possible-world semantics
Pearl incorporates counterfactuals into SCM

relationships.description: This operator is a subtype of the abstract category Epistemic Operator.

specific.transformationRule: computes outcomes under hypothetical interventions

name: Potential Outcomes Framework (Rubin Model)
description: Represents causation through contrasts between potential outcomes (Y₁, Y₀) under different treatments.

chronology.summary: The potential outcomes framework was developed by Donald Rubin in the 1970s (building on Neyman's earlier work). It formalizes causal effects as comparisons of outcomes under treatment and control, and underpins modern causal inference in statistics and econometrics.

events.event: Neyman introduces potential outcomes for randomized experiments
Rubin publishes 'Estimating Causal Effects of Treatments'
Rubin formalizes the 'Rubin Causal Model'
Imbens and Angrist link potential outcomes to instrumental variables

relationships.description: This framework is a subtype of the abstract category Epistemic Framework.

specific.coreAssumptions: Stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA), no interference

name: Causal Bayesian Network
description: Probabilistic graphical models that incorporate interventions as variable manipulations.

chronology.summary: Bayesian networks were introduced by Pearl in the 1980s as a formalism for probabilistic reasoning. The causal interpretation (using do‑calculus) emerged in the 1990s, turning them into Causal Bayesian Networks.

events.event: Pearl publishes 'Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems'
Pearl adds intervention semantics, creating Causal Bayesian Networks

relationships.description: This blueprint is a subtype of the generic causal model blueprint.

expressiveLimits: acyclic
discrete variables (often)

name: Granger Causality
description: X causes Y if past values of X improve prediction of Y beyond Y’s own history.

chronology.summary: Granger causality was proposed by Clive Granger in 1969 as a statistical notion of predictive causality for time series. It became widely used in econometrics and neuroscience, though it is not a true causal model (only predictive).

events.event: Granger publishes 'Investigating Causal Relations by Econometric Models'
Granger receives Nobel Prize for this method

relationships.description: This operator is a subtype of the abstract category Epistemic Operator.

specific.transformationRule: test of predictive improvement via autoregressive models

name: Transfer Entropy
description: Quantifies directional information flow from X to Y.

chronology.summary: Transfer entropy was introduced by Thomas Schreiber in 2000 as an information‑theoretic measure of directed dependency, building on Granger causality and earlier work on mutual information.

events.event: Schreiber publishes 'Measuring Information Transfer'
Transfer entropy linked to Granger causality for Gaussian variables

relationships.description: This operator is a subtype of the abstract category Epistemic Operator.

specific.transformationRule: conditional mutual information between past of X and future of Y

name: Intervention
description: Manipulating one factor to observe change in another; basis for experiments and do-calculus.

chronology.summary: Intervention has been central to experimental science since Bacon. In causal inference, it was formalized by Pearl through the do(·) operator and by Woodward in the manipulationist theory of causation.

events.event: Bacon's 'Novum Organum' emphasizes experimental intervention
Woodward publishes 'Making Things Happen'
Pearl formalizes intervention with do(·) operator

relationships.description: This act is a subtype of the abstract category Epistemic Act.
Intervention acts on causal models.

name: Confounder
description: Influences both cause and effect, potentially biasing causal inference if not controlled for.

chronology.summary: The problem of confounding has been recognized since early statistics (Pearson, Fisher). Formal definitions came from epidemiology and graphical models; Pearl characterized confounders via the back‑door criterion.

events.event: Yule demonstrates spurious correlation due to confounding
Cornfield discusses confounding in epidemiology
Pearl introduces back‑door criterion for confounder control

relationships.description: This constraint is a subtype of the abstract category Epistemic Constraint.
Confounders distort causal effect estimates.

name: Counterfactual (statement)
description: A claim about what would happen if some event had or had not occurred; e.g., 'If A had not occurred, B would not have occurred.'

chronology.summary: Counterfactual statements have been used in philosophy and science for centuries. In causal inference, they are the target of many queries (e.g., 'What would be the outcome if treatment were different?').

events.event: Hume uses counterfactual reasoning
Lewis makes counterfactuals central to his theory of causation
Pearl operationalizes counterfactuals with SCM

relationships.description: This artifact is a subtype of the abstract category Epistemic Artifact.
Counterfactual statements are expressed in causal models.
Counterfactual statements are produced by counterfactual reasoning.

name: Causal Inference
description: Estimating the effects of interventions from observational or experimental data; includes steps like model specification, identification, estimation, and validation.

chronology.summary: Causal inference as a formal discipline grew from statistics (Fisher, Neyman, Rubin) and computer science (Pearl). It is now a standard process in medicine, economics, and AI.

events.event: Fisher introduces randomized experiments
Rubin's potential outcomes framework
Pearl's graphical approach
Causal inference becomes standard in data science

relationships.description: This process is a subtype of the abstract category Epistemic Process.

name: Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT)
description: An experimental design that randomly assigns subjects to treatment/control groups to establish causal relationships.

chronology.summary: RCTs originated in agricultural experiments (Fisher) and biomedical research. They are considered the gold standard for establishing causality because randomization eliminates confounding.

events.event: Fisher introduces randomization in agricultural trials
First modern RCT: streptomycin trial for tuberculosis
RCTs become mandatory for drug approval

name: Causal Discovery
description: Algorithms to learn causal structure (e.g., DAGs) from observational or interventional data.

chronology.summary: Causal discovery emerged from the fusion of graphical models and machine learning in the 1990s. Key algorithms include PC, FCI, and GES, later extended with deep learning.

events.event: Spirtes, Glymour, and Scheines publish 'Causation, Prediction, and Search'
Pearl's IC algorithm
Chickering presents GES (Greedy Equivalence Search)
Deep learning for causal discovery (e.g., DAG-GNN)

name: Against Reification / Layered Causality
description: Causality is not a single mechanism but a bundle of layered processes (biological, social, institutional). Do not treat abstract causal estimates as 'the cause'.

chronology.summary: This principle reflects a critique of naive causal inference that conflates statistical estimates with ontological mechanisms. It draws on systems thinking, critical realism, and philosophy of science (Bhaskar, Cartwright).

events.event: Bhaskar's 'A Realist Theory of Science' critiques causal reification
Cartwright's 'Nature's Capacities and Their Measurement'
Adoption in complex systems and methodologists

relationships.description: This principle is a subtype of the abstract category Epistemic Principle.

specific.formalStatement: Do not treat causal estimates as the unique underlying mechanism

name: Reality Segment
description: Some phenomenon or subset of the real world you want to understand (e.g., physical, biological, social system).

chronology.summary: The notion of a 'piece of reality' as a target of inquiry is implicit in all empirical science. It is a philosophical primitive: the domain that exists independently of representations.

events.event: Aristotle distinguishes substance and accident
Logical positivism's distinction between protocol sentences and reality

relationships.description: This domain is a subtype of the abstract category Epistemic Domain.

name: Barnes–Hut Simulation
description: A computational epistemic process implementing the Barnes–Hut algorithm to simulate large-scale N-body dynamical systems through hierarchical spatial decomposition and approximate force aggregation.

chronology.summary: Developed in 1986 by Josh Barnes and Piet Hut to address computational inefficiency in N-body simulations, the Barnes–Hut method became foundational in computational astrophysics and large-scale force simulation.

events.event: Barnes and Hut publish hierarchical tree algorithm
Broad adoption in galaxy and cosmological simulations
Extension into GPU and distributed architectures

relationships.description: Implements recursive spatial decomposition for computational efficiency.
Uses the Barnes–Hut algorithm as its formal computational operator.
Expresses simulation state and partitioning through hierarchical tree blueprints.
Bounded by timestep stability, force approximation error, and finite precision.
Produces evolving concrete epistemic artifacts representing system trajectories.
Evaluated through conservation laws, error analysis, and simulation robustness.
Depends on computational infrastructure for scalability.

specific.validationMethod: Numerical convergence analysis, physical conservation checks, approximation error benchmarking
functionalRoles: Transformation of initial state artifacts into temporal state trajectories

categoryAmbiguity.primaryJustification: Primarily classified as an epistemic process because it is an ordered operational activity transforming inputs into validated predictive artifacts over time.

alternativeCategories.justification: The Barnes–Hut algorithm itself functions as a transformation operator.
Can also function as part of broader computational simulation frameworks.
Specific simulation instances produce fully specified predictive artifacts.

name: Algorithm
description: A formally specified, finite, ordered sequence of operations that transforms defined inputs into outputs according to explicit procedural rules.

chronology.summary: Algorithms emerged from early mathematical procedures and were formally generalized through logic, computability theory, and modern computer science.

events.event: Euclidean procedural mathematics
Al-Khwarizmi's procedural arithmetic methods
Turing formalizes computation through Turing machines
Modern computational algorithmics expands

relationships.description: Algorithms operationalize formal logical or mathematical principles into executable procedures.
Algorithms are encoded through procedural blueprints such as pseudocode, flowcharts, or programming languages.
Algorithms transform structured epistemic artifacts into new informational states.
Algorithmic performance is constrained by time, space, and tractability limitations.
Algorithms enable broader epistemic processes such as modeling, inference, experimentation, and optimization.

specific.transformationRule: Executes a finite sequence of formally defined state transformations from input to output.
specific.operandType: symbolic, numeric, logical, or physical representations
specific.computationalComplexity: Varies by implementation and problem class

categoryAmbiguity.primaryJustification: Algorithm is primarily an epistemic operator because its defining feature is formal transformation of representations via executable procedural rules.

alternativeCategories.justification: Algorithms may also be treated as abstract representational procedural structures independent of execution.
When instantiated temporally in real systems, algorithms function as operational processes.
Certain algorithms encode adaptive search or optimization strategies.

metadata.sourceReference: Conceptual synthesis from computability theory, computer science, systems theory, and epistemology.

auditTrail.reviewNote: Initial formalization of algorithm as an epistemic operator with category ambiguity analysis.

name: ElectromagneticWave
description: A self-propagating transverse wave of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that travels through vacuum or matter at the speed of light, carrying energy and momentum without requiring a material medium.

chronology.summary: The concept of electromagnetic waves emerged from the unification of electricity and magnetism by James Clerk Maxwell in the 1860s, who predicted their existence. Heinrich Hertz experimentally generated and detected radio waves in 1887, confirming Maxwell's theory. Later developments included the discovery of X-rays by Röntgen (1895), gamma rays by Villard (1900), and the quantum formulation by Einstein (1905) and others, leading to wave-particle duality.

events.event: Maxwell publishes 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field', predicting electromagnetic waves.
events.associatedContext: Unification of electricity, magnetism, and light; wave equation derived.

events.event: Hertz experimentally generates and detects radio waves, confirming Maxwell's prediction.
events.associatedContext: First controlled production and measurement of electromagnetic waves in the laboratory.

events.event: Einstein explains the photoelectric effect using light quanta (photons), introducing wave-particle duality.
events.associatedContext: Quantum nature challenges purely classical wave ontology.

relationships.description: An electromagnetic wave is composed of oscillating electric and magnetic fields mutually inducing each other.
The behavior of electromagnetic waves is formalized by Maxwell's equations in vacuum or media.
Electromagnetic waves produce radiation pressure and momentum transfer upon absorption or reflection.

specific.conceptEvaluationNote: The electromagnetic wave is a highly successful ontic concept in classical physics, enabling precise predictions of propagation, interference, and radiation. However, at quantum scales it is supplanted by the photon field description, though classical waves remain a valid approximation for many phenomena (coherent states). As an epistemic tool, it provides an intuitive visualizable model but must be complemented by quantum field theory for completeness.

categoryAmbiguity.primaryJustification: Electromagnetic wave is a fundamental ontic entity in classical electromagnetism, directly referring to a real physical phenomenon, not an epistemic artifact or process.

metadata.sourceReference: Derived from Maxwell's equations, standard electrodynamics textbooks (e.g., Jackson, Griffiths), and historical analysis.

name: Number
description: An abstract symbolic and structural construct used to represent quantity, magnitude, order, relation, ratio, measure, and formal mathematical structure.

chronology.summary: The concept of number evolved from primitive counting systems into increasingly abstract mathematical structures used across scientific, computational, and formal domains.

events.event: Primitive tally systems emerge
events.associatedContext: Early human counting and resource tracking

events.event: Babylonian positional numeral systems develop
Greek mathematical abstraction of numbers
Formalization of zero and arithmetic rules in India
Expansion of real and complex number systems
Cantor develops set-theoretic foundations of cardinality
events.associatedContext: Infinite set theory and formal mathematics

events.event: Formal computational treatment of numbers

specific.formalism: Arithmetic, algebraic, logical, set-theoretic, and computational formal systems
expressiveLimits: Cannot fully represent continuous physical reality with finite precision
Dependent on formal axiomatic systems
Some numerical truths are undecidable within formal systems
Finite computational representations introduce approximation and rounding errors
Symbolic representation may diverge from ontological structure of reality
functionalRoles: Act as operands in computational systems
Enable abstraction of physical and conceptual systems

categoryAmbiguity.primaryJustification: The concept of number is classified primarily as an epistemicBlueprint because it functions as a formal representational structure used to model and manipulate quantitative relationships across domains.

alternativeCategories.justification: Numbers serve operational roles as operands within transformation systems.
Numerals and written numerical symbols exist as concrete symbolic artifacts.
Entire mathematical systems may organize around numerical structures.
Certain philosophical traditions treat numbers as ontologically real entities.

metadata.sourceReference: Synthetic conceptual synthesis derived from mathematics, philosophy of mathematics, logic, computation theory, and epistemology.

auditTrail.reviewNote: Initial conceptual formalization of the number concept using the Conceptual Structure Typing Node Schema.

name: Decision Theory
description: A formal epistemic framework that structures how rational agents select actions under uncertainty by integrating preferences, beliefs, and probabilistic reasoning into decision rules.

chronology.summary: Emerges from utility theory, probability theory, and formal economics.

events.event: Expected utility foundation (Bernoulli)
Axiomatic expected utility theory (von Neumann & Morgenstern)

relationships.description: Operationalizes probabilistic coherence in belief updating and decision evaluation.

specific.coreAssumptions: Agents act to maximize expected utility under probabilistic beliefs; preferences are coherent and transitive; uncertainty is representable via probability distributions.
specific.integrationScope: Integrates probability theory, utility theory, optimization, and game theory into a unified decision architecture.

references.title: Expected Utility Theory (von Neumann & Morgenstern)
references.description: Foundational axiomatic formulation of decision-making under risk.

references.title: A Treatise on Probability - John Maynard Keynes
references.description: Early formal treatment of probabilistic reasoning in decision contexts.

name: Decision-Making
description: A structured epistemic process in which an agent selects one action from a set of alternatives based on evaluation of expected outcomes, constraints, and objectives.

chronology.summary: Studied across psychology, economics, and artificial intelligence as a core rationality process.

events.event: Bounded rationality (Herbert Simon)

relationships.description: Implements decision theory as the guiding evaluative framework.
Constrained by incomplete information and stochastic environments.

specific.validationMethod: Outcome evaluation against realized utility and prediction error minimization

references.title: Administrative Behavior - Herbert A. Simon
references.description: Foundational work on bounded rationality in decision processes.

name: Decision Problem
description: A structured representational schema defining the components of a decision situation: states, actions, outcomes, and evaluation criteria.

chronology.summary: Evolved from early economic modeling and operations research formulations.

relationships.description: Serves as input specification for decision-making processes.

specific.formalism: ⟨S, A, P, U⟩ formal decision tuple
expressiveLimits: Requires explicit enumeration or parametrization of states and actions
May struggle with high-dimensional continuous spaces without approximation

references.title: Markov Decision Processes in Operations Research
references.description: Formal framework for sequential decision problems under uncertainty.

name: Action Space
description: The structured set of all feasible actions available to an agent within a decision context.

chronology.summary: Originates in control theory and mathematical decision models.

relationships.description: Forms a component of the decision problem structure.

specific.formalism: A ∈ ℝⁿ or discrete set A = {a₁, a₂, ..., aₙ}
expressiveLimits: May become intractable in high-dimensional continuous spaces
Requires discretization or sampling in complex systems

references.title: Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction - Sutton & Barto
references.description: Standard reference for action spaces in sequential decision systems.

name: Utility Function
description: A formal mapping from states or outcomes to scalar values representing preference intensity.

chronology.summary: Developed in utility theory and expected value formalizations.

relationships.description: Serves as a parameterized component within decision theory.

specific.formalism: U: S → ℝ or U: (S × A) → ℝ
expressiveLimits: Assumes comparability of all outcomes via scalar reduction
May fail under preference intransitivity or context dependence

references.title: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior
references.description: Foundational formalization of utility functions in economics.

name: Uncertainty Constraint
description: A limiting condition in which incomplete or stochastic information restricts the determinacy of inference and decision outcomes.

chronology.summary: Central to probability theory and statistical inference.

relationships.description: Restricts accuracy and determinacy of decision-making processes.

specific.failureMode: misestimation, variance explosion, incorrect inference under missing data

references.title: Probability Theory: The Logic of Science - Jaynes
references.description: Foundational treatment of uncertainty in inference and decision-making.

name: No-go Theorem
description: A no-go theorem is a formal mathematical result demonstrating that a particular combination of assumptions necessarily precludes a certain desired outcome, imposing a fundamental limit on what can be achieved within a given framework.

chronology.summary: The concept of a no-go theorem emerged in early 20th-century foundational debates, notably von Neumann's 1932 attempt to exclude hidden variables from quantum mechanics. It was later sharpened by Bell (1964), Kochen–Specker (1967), and extended to relativistic causality, quantum information, and computability theory.

events.event: von Neumann publishes 'Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics', containing an impossibility proof for hidden-variable theories.
Bell's theorem demonstrates that no local hidden-variable theory can reproduce all quantum predictions.
Wootters, Zurek, and Dieks independently prove the no-cloning theorem.

relationships.description: No-go Theorem is a subclass of epistemic constraint that formalizes impossibility within a defined axiomatic system.

specific.boundedResource: space of physically or logically possible states/operations
specific.failureMode: contradiction with fundamental axioms if the outcome were achievable

references.title: The No-Cloning Theorem
references.description: Seminal paper proving that an arbitrary unknown quantum state cannot be copied perfectly.

name: No Free Lunch Theorem
description: The No Free Lunch (NFL) theorem states that all optimization algorithms perform equally well when averaged over all possible objective functions, implying that no algorithm is universally superior without problem-specific structural assumptions.

chronology.summary: Published by David Wolpert and William Macready in 1997, the NFL theorems provided a rigorous formalization of the long-held intuition that there is no universally best optimizer. Subsequent work extended the results to co-evolution, supervised learning, and other search domains.

events.event: Wolpert and Macready publish 'No Free Lunch Theorems for Optimization' in IEEE Transactions on Evolutionary Computation.

relationships.description: The No Free Lunch Theorem is a concrete instance of an epistemic constraint bounding algorithmic generalization.

specific.boundedResource: expected optimization performance across all objective functions
specific.failureMode: vanishing advantage of any algorithm over random search when problem distribution is uniform

references.title: No Free Lunch Theorems for Optimization
references.description: Original paper establishing the foundational impossibility result for optimization algorithms.

name: Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman Equation
description: The Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation is a partial differential equation that provides a necessary and sufficient condition for optimality in continuous-time optimal control problems, expressing the value function in terms of system dynamics, cost function, and control policy.

chronology.summary: Evolving from the classical Hamilton-Jacobi equation of mechanics, the HJB equation was developed in the mid-20th century after Richard Bellman introduced dynamic programming. It became a cornerstone of continuous-time optimal control, alongside Pontryagin's maximum principle.

events.event: Richard Bellman develops the principle of optimality and dynamic programming.
The Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation is formalized for continuous-time stochastic and deterministic optimal control.

relationships.description: The HJB equation is a specific encoding format (partial differential equation blueprint) within optimal control.

expressiveLimits: requires continuous differentiability of the value function
curse of dimensionality in numerical discretization
assumes Markovian dynamics and full state observability

references.title: Dynamic Programming
references.description: Bellman’s foundational text introducing the principle of optimality and the value function approach.
